To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions caused by the underwater cable's dispersion. To address these limitations, the introduction of optimized pulse patterns is proposed, showcasing a significant improvement in BER performance across various sea conditions. Notably, the weighted DFE technique still exhibits some advantages and could be hybridized with the new pulse pattern for further enhanced performance. Moreover, the feasibility of this transmission system is validated through a range of measurements during actual underwater transmissions. To further analyze the limitations of this transmission system, a numerical model incorporating the effects of fading, burst errors, and fiber attenuation is developed, indicating that the system's BER could be improved by increasing the codeword length and employing more efficient error-correction codes. Additionally, the development of more sophisticated equalizer techniques, such as blind and adaptive FE equalizers, is also advocated. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for the design of next-generation submarine fiber communications systems. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Additionally, it is proposed that future experiments with the LHC's higher collision energies will be able to pinpoint fluctuations in $v_3$ and potentially those in $v_1$. Lastly, it is suggested that $v_1$ fluctuations could serve as a direct indicator of collisions' asymmetry and associated collective behavior. In such cases, researchers propose utilizing three-particle correlations instead of two-particle correlations due to the former's increased sensitivity to $v_1$ fluctuations. This could also provide valuable insights into $v_1$ behavior and its relationship with $v_3$ behavior across different centralities and the momentum of the particles. Furthermore, it is predicted that in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 3 GeV/c, fluctuations in $v_3$ will dominate over those in $v_1$. This understanding could offer a glimpse into quark--gluon plasma's behavior during these collisions and potentially aid in developing new strategies for utilizing collective flow as a tool to study quark--gluon plasma's internal structure. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This dual approach for ALBA's rules on DLEs forms the basis for our proof of several canonicity properties, including a universally applicable one that connects every inductive formula with a specific syntactic form to its associated first-order correspondent. Central to our proof is the demonstration of how the algebraic language associated with ALBA's rules cuts across different DLEs, leading to an intriguing generalization of the correspondence theory. Furthermore, we showcase the applicability of this inverse approach in establishing novel canonicity results within the boundaries of the universal fragment of modal logic. Additionally, we explore the limitations of this inverse method by examining an existing complexity barrier, as well as a range of open questions arising from our findings. The overall exploration and results achieved through the inverse application of ALBA's rules raise intriguing questions and opportunities for further research within the field. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison

Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic simulation process, mimicking the process used in actual cameras. By doing so, we demonstrate the superiority of our single-stage model over traditional approaches and complex optimization-based methods, with the benefit of significantly reduced computational overhead. Our results show that our method not only surpasses these alternatives in terms of subjective quality, but also achieves superior objective quality metrics. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be adapted to handle partially blurred and noisy raw images, resulting in a versatile framework that outperforms state-of-the-art methods tailored to specific deblurring and demosaicking applications. Our code and data are publicly available for download. Additionally, we have introduced a new Raw Image Quality Assessment (RIQA) task, along with a corresponding dataset containing a variety of distorted raw images, along with their corresponding quality scores. This dataset is also made available for download. We achieved the lowest PSNR and SSIM scores with both single-stage models, except for the case where only deblurring was evaluated. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. The research with its accompanying analysis provides a framework for better understanding the complex dynamics of water-entry surface seal in spheres. Furthermore, it suggests that both nonlinear elasticity and water-cavity interactions contribute significantly to influencing pressures within the formed cavity, leading to increased pressures at mid-range speeds. The pressuring within the water-filled cavity raises the sphere's overall, making it more resistant to further penetration, and ultimately results in the closure of the formed splash dome. In essence, when a sphere enters water at mid-range speeds, the pressure within the cavity pushes the surrounding water up, creating a seal that delays pinch-off time. In fact, the pressure within the cavity is so great that it overcomes the sphere's original downward momentum, slowing its further penetration, and ultimately contributing to the closure of the formed dome. In water-entry surface seal regime, both the partial-seal, and secondary pinch-off stages demonstrate similar pressure behavior, and therefore share the same underlying dynamics. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board, which demonstrates the efficacy of our approach in secure data protection. 
Additionally, we include analytical evaluations and comparative assessments with existing security-centric architectures. 

This research, encompassing both hardware and software components, is now part of the OctopOS open-source platform, available for public access. 
We have also included user-guided instruction on setting up the device. 
Furthermore, we have conducted a user-study, detailing the results, to demonstrate the feasibility of this security-oriented architecture for everyday mobile device applications. 
With this approach, we have successfully reduced the necessary hardware components by 45%, power consumption by 30%, and cost by 50% compared to existing security-focused architectures while still delivering comparable performance. 
On top of that, we have realized a notable performance boost of 30% in mobile applications with heavy security processing. 
Finally, we have successfully incorporated machine learning applications into this secure architecture, showcasing the versatility of this innovative hardware and software design. 
Despite enhancing security, we have not introduced any significant learning for manufacturers to incorporate into their manufacturing process. 
Consequently, this design is suitable for a wide range of mobile device manufacturers. 
On the software side, we have tackled several key challenges – namely, scheduling, virtual machine management, network stack re-design, and user interface component integration. 
Lastly, we have included several popular mobile security applications, as well as anti-virus software, on top of this architecture, further demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness. 
Overall, this innovative hardware and software design has successfully reduced trust requirements, making secure mobile devices more affordable, efficient, and accessible to a wider population.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The code for the proposed FPG algorithm is publicly available at the specified repository link. Leveraging the results of FPG, we also established the limitations of reinforcement learning when transition corruption exceeds $O(1)$ and discussed strategies to enhance its performance. Additionally, we explored the applicability of reinforcement learning to safety-critical domains. The theoretical and practical achievements of robust reinforcement learning are valuable contributions to the field. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Additionally, we outline the requirements for implementing SPCCSs using quantum-optical catalysis with linear optics and homodyne detection. SPCCSs present an appealing option for employing coherent states in quantum information processing and communication protocols. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. We demonstrate how the implementation of direct transcription led to viable patient ventilation strategies. Furthermore, we emphasize the crucial role of simulation-based annotation in reducing the dimensionality of this complex problem, thus facilitating successful solution finding with minimal transcendental function evaluations. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in solving demanding nonlinear dynamic optimization problems. Additionally, we highlight the significance of collaboration between control theory and practical engineering expertise in resolving real-world challenges. We conclude that the ability to formulate problems in the form of nonlinear dynamic optimization makes direct transcription a valuable tool for solving complex engineering problems of control, estimation, and design. Our case study and the positive outcomes obtained underscore the utility of this technique in tackling real-world applications. Finally, we propose that researchers and practitioners with experience in nonlinear dynamic optimization should contribute their expertise in solving complex engineering problems of control, estimation, and design. In addition, we highlight the necessity for clear, concise, and concise language in presenting technical research to a diverse audience. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in resolving a critical engineering challenge related to patient ventilation. Additionally, we emphasize the benefits of collaborating with industry partners and the importance of preserving the anonymity of subjects participating in experimental data collection process. Lastly, we suggest considering government funding sources for collaborative research projects and emphasize the value of working with experienced research assistants. Moreover, we highlight the benefits of attending prestigious scientific conferences and the importance of upholding academic integrity by properly citing sources in research papers. Finally, we outline potential future research projects, including potential solutions to the ventilator shortage, the development of a patient-specific ventilation system, and novel methods for estimating unknown parameters with measurement data. We conclude by expressing our gratitude to our research collaborators and highlight the benefits of working with a diverse team of graduate students.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Additionally, in areas with a conservative voter base, we found increased dissemination of misinformation from conservative and mixed news sources, while in areas with a diverse population, we found increased circulation of misinformation from liberal and mixed news sources. Our findings suggest that The Big Sort may contribute substantially to the enhanced spread of misinformation observed in recent years. We also explored potential interventions, concluding that targeting specific geographic areas with reliable information campaigns could be an effective strategy in containing misinformation dissemination. However, such strategies may be less successful at decreasing overall misinformation spread rates due to inherent supply-chain dynamics. Finally, we recommend researchers and practitioners collaborate to study and address online misinformation more comprehensively. Additionally, we provide guidelines and open-data resources for replication of our research and exploration of additional aspects of this pressing issue. Nonetheless, we caution against generalizing our findings beyond the specific context and platform examined in this study. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. This research's findings can be utilized to develop more effective speech-based interfaces for interacting with robots in a human-friendly manner and to inform the design of robotic systems capable of effectively learning from auditory feedback during demonstrations and other instructions. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. These limitations impose significant constraints on the development of an efficient test generator. To overcome these constraints, developers rely on alternative approaches, such as leveraging human input, incorporating existing test cases, and utilising existing test agents. We also explore the scope, design, and implementation details of our testing framework, including our approach to specifying test cases, executing tests, and updating the test suite. Finally, we discuss the pros and cons of this implementation, as well as potential avenues for improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the test generator. This research is a crucial step towards creating a comprehensive testing environment for conversational agents, and we anticipate that our findings will be invaluable to the community. This concept has already been incorporated into the DialogBumper suite, an open-source dataset designed for testing conversational systems. This suite comprises a test generator, test cases, and a set of developed models, all of which can be accessed through https://github.com/omerg/DialogBumper/. This dataset places demands on the quality of the generated text, diversity of test cases, and model performance, thereby setting a high standard for future advancements in this area. Due to the limited scope of our research, we have excluded other crucial aspects of software systems, such as data management, system integration, and security features, from the testing framework. Nonetheless, we believe that our work has significant implications, and we look forward to collaborating with other researchers and practitioners in this field. Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we discovered a previously overlooked component in the CMB, describing power fluctuations in the 5-11 degree range, which could be related to CCCE anomalies. Our study highlights the importance of further investigating non-linear patterns in the CMB to better understand the early universe. Additionally, we observed seasonal anomalies in solar radiation, which may influence low-energy experiments, and suggest that researchers and scientists should be aware of these seasonal fluctuations when interpreting data and conducting experiments. Our analysis and research strategies have been made publicly available, and we invite the scientific community to build upon and contribute to our study. Our findings and conclusions are based on two independent analyses, and we believe that our results, although not supporting the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model, can still advance our understanding of the universe. Moreover, we anticipate that future satellite missions, such as CMB-S4, will be capable of conducting in-depth analyses of the CMB with improved resolution and sensitivity. Until then, we propose using existing data to test theoretical models and search for CCCE signatures and anomalies. Our primary goal is to inspire a renewed interest in exploring the universe's complex phenomena and to motivate the development of more sophisticated analytical tools. Additionally, we hope that our study will contribute to a greater recognition of the importance of interdisciplinary research and the value of open data sharing and research collaborations. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR achieves a comprehensive understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets consistently demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, MSDCR's scalability and flexibility make it particularly suitable for the ever-changing and dynamic environment characteristic of online multi-domain recommendation scenarios. It offers fast, byte-granular data access similar to DRAM, combined with power-fail safe storage. In-depth performance evaluations have shown Optane DC PMMs to excel as primary memory and persistent storage accessible by user-level applications. Various modes and benchmarks have been used to measure Optane DC PMMs performance under different scenarios, including comparison to DRAM, which revealed the following results. When used with a DRAM cache to mask their relatively slow bandwidth, applications with small memory footprints are largely unaffected. Those requiring more storage may experience some performance degradation but still benefit from retaining more data in memory. In file system mode, especially with optimizations tailored to the Optane DC PMMs load/store interface, significant performance improvements were achieved, up to two times the performance with certain applications. Furthermore, user-level applications with Optane DC persistence outperformed those using the file system approach, resulting in substantial time gains. In specific instances, user-level applications with Optane DC persistence outperformed those using the file system approach by almost two times. In addition, in scenarios where the system does not lose power, Optane DC PMMs can function similarly to DRAM with minimal performance differences. In contrast, traditional flash storage, which requires a reboot after a power failure and introduces various latencies, cannot match the performance of memory or storage provided by the Optane DC PMM during a prolonged power outage. Nonetheless, it still offers a significant advantage over flash storage. In instances where data loss during a power failure is acceptable, Optane DC PMMs can serve as cost-effective, fast, and persistent storage with superior performance compared to flash storage. In scenarios where data loss during a power failure is unacceptable, additional hardware components are needed to provide reliable storage and ensure that critical data is safely stored across power failures. In such cases, Optane DC PMMs can function as fast primary memory with storage capabilities that provide valuable application performance gains, particularly in applications that can benefit from retaining more data in memory or reducing file system latency. For each family, it predicts a wide range of particles, including 22 new quarks, 18 new leptons, 61 new gauge bosons, 59 new scalars, and 29 new vectors. Calculations for the masses of these predicted particles yield the following results: all quarks and leptons are expected to have masses similar to that of an electron, or be too heavy to be discovered with current technology. Conversely, calculations for the masses of the predicted bilepton model mesons yield the following results: some will likely weigh as much as a proton, or even heavier. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. Consequently, we have developed the APPLGRAPH/WebAPPLGRAPH framework to automate this process, allowing which allows users to define process flow based on input and output quantities, supported by an graphical user interface. Additionally, we have created an instance of this framework, suited for the DT PDF fitting initiative, which incorporates various process and density functions computations, driven by physical constraints and experimental data. This implementation is available for download at https://dt-pdf.org/applgraph/. We encourage users to submit their own process definitions utilizing the provided Python API, and we look forward to contributing this development to the statistical community. Finally, we have been inspired by the ideas presented in this project to integrate the evolution equations with the Weyl unitary group, leading to the development of the CCSDS-LA format, a unified standard for PDF representations that can facilitate cross-comparisons and combinations of different density functions. This format is also introduced in this paper. We have been awarded funding from the CTS3 consortium to further develop this project in collaboration with the University of Oxford, the University of Southampton, and the University of Durham. Specifically, we aim to enhance the interpretability of the results obtained with this framework, especially with regards to cross-section predictions, and to establish a public forum for discussion and exchange of ideas among research groups working on PDF fitting. Additionally, we plan to organize workshops and conferences, and to establish a repository for openly sharing results obtained with this framework, as well as any new developments made to it. We have already been invited to present this project at the 2019 PDF4FIT meeting, and we look forward to presenting it at the 2020 APPA meeting. We have also been invited to become a part of the DT PDF fitting initiative, led by the University of Durham, and we have been awarded funding from the University of Oxford to further develop this project

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Furthermore, our spin-lattice relaxation studies revealed a direct proportionality between the measured relaxation times and those of LaAlO$_3$ substrates, indicating that LaNiO$_3$ protons play a significant role in spin-lattice relaxation. Additionally, our measurements observed a pronounced anisotropy in spin diffusion, with faster recovery times observed when LaNiO$_3$ layers are perpendicular to the applied radio frequency field. This anisotropy is more pronounced at higher temperatures and is believed to result from enhanced spin-lattice interactions along the c-axis in LaNiO$_3$. Our findings contribute significantly to the understanding of LaNiO$_3$ physics and have important implications for other correlated metals with volatile protons. Additionally, our study suggests that $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR holds great promise as a tool for investigating the physics of these materials. Nonetheless, accessing higher magnetic fields is essential to fully explore the spin-lattice relaxation studies in these materials. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We also show that the latter can be interpreted through the lens of conformal field theory. Specifically, we find that the restrictions of these Gaussian free fields to curves of time $t$ can be seen as random variables with a specific distribution, namely the highest weight character of the representation of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ at a specific central charge, $\frac{3}{2}$. This resolution of the imaginary surface framework using stochastic processes allows for the application of tools from probability and analysis, such as the Bessis-McKean-Zhang convolution theorem, to the study of the underlying processes. Additionally, we observe that the distribution of these random variables exhibits multifragmentary behavior. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocity approach in radio astronomy can be utilized. By analyzing the velocity of radio emission from binary star systems, researchers can gather valuable information about their internal structure and the gravitational force that holds them together. Conversely, any line velocity observed is a combination of the movement of the binary star system and its surrounding space. While it is possible to dissect this velocity distribution, doing so is complicated by several factors, including the limited knowledge of the line velocity profile, the binary star system's orientation, and its velocity trajectory. Nonetheless, even without fully understanding these velocity distributions, the line velocity approach offers a key advantage over other methods. Typically, the velocity of binary star systems is measured using optical observations of their movement across the sky, a method that is susceptible to systematic errors associated with the line velocity profile. In contrast, radio observations of the line velocity provide a more direct velocity measurement, uncorrelated with the line velocity profile. To employ the line velocity approach in radio observations, the 21cm radio line, which originates from hydrogen atoms within the binary star system's surrounding interstellar cloud, is ideal. However, to accurately interpret the results, considerations must be given to any gravitational field affecting the radio emission on its path to the observer, a factor that could potentially mask the binary star system's velocity distribution. To minimize such uncertainties, researchers can select binary star systems located near the edge of the surrounding interstellar cloud. By doing so, they can significantly reduce the volume of space being studied, thereby limiting the possible velocity distributions that could explain the observed data. As a result, future radio observations of the 21cm line from these binary star systems hold great promise in determining how gravity behaves at low acceleration rates. Furthermore, incorporating pulsar rotation measures can enhance the sensitivity of these systems to the law of gravity, while new radio surveys of the line velocity towards these binary star systems are anticipated to yield significant results. Additionally, the detection of the 21cm line from these systems using the Square Kilometre Array will provide a broader perspective, offering a wider range of environmental conditions and varying timescales over several decades. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview. Building on the foundations laid in Part 1, we in Part 2 explore more advanced topics in $\tau$-tilting theory. We examine how $\tau$-tilting factors incorporate representation theory into the structure theory of finite-dimensional algebras, followed by in-depth analyses of the relationships between $\tau$-tilting modules, $\tau$-tilting functors, and the Cohen-Macaulay property. We also discuss how $\tau$-tilting theory can be applied to various classes of algebras and cover the results on the $\tau$-tilting frame of an algebra, including its growth, as well as the development of the local $\tau$-tilting theory. Additionally, we explore Ext-$\tau$-tilting theory and the connections between $\tau$-tilting theory and cluster-tilted algebras. We conclude by reviewing the results on the representation theory of higher finite-dimensional algebras and discussing the representation theory of infinite-dimensional algebras. Lastly, we address the current challenges and potential future directions in the field. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. This study introduces an algorithm capable of identifying whether breaking a limited number of nodes in a bipartite graph allows for an edge-free representation and, if so, plans an optimal subset of nodes to break. Additionally, this algorithm's efficiency makes it suitable for application in fixed-parameter theorem proving. Parameters, such as graph density and the size of the largest connected component, do not significantly affect the algorithm's performance. A key innovation in this algorithm employs a novel approach to evaluating whether combining two disjoint subgraphs results in a planar combination, leveraging a new set of bipartite graphs characterized by specific structural properties, thereby breaking the symmetry typically inherent in integrated splitting problems. Moreover, this algorithm provides optimal solutions for splitting node pairs, a more complex variant, and can be adapted to other contexts, such as planarizing graphs using node mergings. Experimental implementations have shown this algorithm's effectiveness in tackling real-world data sets. The implementation and data sets used in this research are available online. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to store examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes learned are representative of all previous data, although such retention comes with a cost in computational resources. We investigated a wide range of techniques for weight calibration and compared their performance in this specific context. The techniques we explored include different optimization methods such as contrastive learning, adversarial training, and reinforcement learning. We also examined direct loss function modification through over-sampling the underrepresented classes and applying an imbalance weight. These techniques were assessed in the context of a dataset that models real-world data streams, characterized by constant and sudden data arrivals. The evaluation showed that the simplest yet most effective approaches yielded the best performance. We found that the performance gained from weight calibration techniques is not sufficient to compensate for the performance degradation resulting from forgetting older classes and data. Moreover, the benefits of these techniques may not offset the storage requirements. We made our code and dataset accessible via publicly available repositories. Finally, we highlighted key implications for future research derived from our findings. With the anticipated growth of IoT applications and the continuous influx of video streams, there is a pressing need to address the challenges posed by imbalanced class incremental learning. One potential avenue to explore is adapting the deep neural network architecture in response to incoming data and incorporating all data samples from previously encountered classes into the memory store. Additionally, more comprehensive evaluation protocols are also needed to ensure the robustness of evaluations. Due to the limited scale and diversity of current open datasets related to learning in streams and big datasets, there is a need for larger and more diverse data sets that model real-world scenarios. One such dataset, called the Large Class Incremental Learning dataset, was created as part of this research. One key characteristic of this dataset is that it encompasses a wide variety of classes and incorporates data from multiple data sources. Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. This, however, is in contrast to a previous result of the authors, which indicated that, for complex scalars, the residue map induces an surjective connection between two related fields of power series and thus suggested that these fields should be equivalent. This paper provides an explanation for this discrepancy by identifying a fundamental limitation applicable across all non-trivially valued fields of the type in question. This limitation renders the associated theory with a specific additional property as essentially equivalent to a specific finite theory and thus guarantee that it meets another specific property. Furthermore, this solution also provides an alternative proof for the undecidability of another previously mentioned field of power series. This research was initially presented as a talk at the 2012 model theory conference in Munster. In the course of his research, Winkler obtained some additional results, which are also included in this paper, and for his benefit, the paper is now being published in its current form. In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.  The implementation and testing of HyperDegrade-based attacks on multiple platforms and protocols are made available through an open-source attack framework, which showcases the technique's versatility and effectiveness.  Finally, suggestions for securing against such attacks via the implementation of low-latency, hardware-based mitigation techniques and alterations to how software is deployed are offered as potential improvements, which could potentially provide better protection against these types of attacks.  However, these suggestions are left as ideas for future research. Specifically, we focus on SCET and LLA, highlighting their underlying principles and applications. We also address concerns regarding amplitude-based resummation, specifically massless high-energy extensions and the beam thrust approach, and discuss the implications of "non-logarithmic amplitudes," highlighting the importance of direct calculations or integral representations. We emphasize that in field theory, infrared divergences originate from ultraviolet divergences, and therefore, infrared improvement of amplitudes is guaranteed. We examine the beam thrust effective field theory as a promising approach to handle multi-particle final states and discuss the promising outcomes from preliminary studies at the LHC and future colliders. We conclude that further research is needed to fully understand the capabilities and limitations of amplitude-based resummation and to fully realize its potential in the development of precision theoretical predictions. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package called PyFTX for the beam thrust effective field theory, which can be used as a template for user applications. This package is now available on GitHub and can be used as a starting point for user codes. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to collaborate on modeling real global data. Typically, entities share partial information about their own data when contributing to a shared federated learning model. Here we investigate a privacy threat that can be observed when entities participate in the required training process for their data shares. Specifically, we demonstrate how to statistically analyze and numerically quantify the privacy leakage for participants in vertical federated learning. Our results show that the privacy leakage is noticeable and can be as high as 90% for certain data types. Consequently, our findings suggest that, without sufficient data encryption, entities may be unwilling to collaborate. Finally, we highlight the importance of addressing these privacy concerns to maintain trust among data contributors. In the process, we also compare the privacy leakage in horizontal and vertical federated learning setups, revealing that the latter results in significantly greater privacy risks. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. Our results indicate that the proposed approach yields superior performance in multiple metrics, including efficiency, accuracy, and generically, across real-world datasets. Furthermore, this method exhibits predictive patterns that indicate its potential for efficient handling of big data sets. Our implementation is included as an open source Python module, readily available for use. In particular, we provide our implementation's code at https://github.com/amir-arad/psrf features, and it is also integrated into scikit-learn's kernel approximation module as version 0.24. Additionally, we include an in-depth analysis and comparison of our proposed method with multiple alternative methods, including both traditional and more recent approaches. This analysis is presented in the form of an interactive visualization tool, also made available at https://kernel-approximation-analysis.org. This study's key findings are summarized in the form of an easily accessible, data, as presented in https://kernel-approximation-analysis.org/data. Finally, we outline potential future research directions inspired by our analysis and kernel approximation in general, specifically in relation to the choice of base kernel and the development of data-dependent feature mapping methods. This study's scope encompasses real-valued kernel methods, including multiclass classification and regression applications. Additionally, we explore potential extensions to complex-valued domains, primarily inspired by our results. Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Our findings also highlight that modern detection benchmarks are heavily dominated by mid-scale objects, which pose significant challenges for models that have not been scaled up in proportion with the data. As a result, all models tested require additional training on the full 80,000-image COCO dataset to achieve optimal performance on large-scale objects. Ultimately, this work emphasizes the necessity for more balanced, easily accessible, and widely applicable detection datasets that cover a more practical range of object scales. This expanded dataset, referred to as COCO-Scale (COS), is now available for public use. From the perspective of mirror symmetry, these high-dimensional non-toric varieties establish the Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for our current knowledge limits. Building upon this foundation, 48 more $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been constructed, with their depth spanning between 10 and 19. We investigate the concurrent loss of spatial translation and dilation symmetries in a class of models inspired by the Ginzburg-Landau theory, in which the mechanisms responsible for symmetry breaking are represented by a potential function describing spatial gradients. Our research reveals the existence of modes with subdimensional or zero propagation, characterized as "fractons", where their motion is constrained. The effective field theories of this type encompass systems like helical superfluids and metafluids, in which fractons can be linked to an underlying symmetry associated with higher order charges, resulting in the simplification of some elastic properties. Introducing a finite charge density influences the fracton's mobility, leading to a trade-off between the chemical potential and superfluid velocity in determining the gap of the dilaton. The mobility of fractons can also be modified at zero density by incorporating higher derivative terms. These considerations imply that the conformal field theories describing systems with broken translation and dilation symmetries may exhibit mobility gaps in the dilaton and helical metafluids. The models studied here demonstrate that the loss of these symmetries leads to the creation of fractons with distinct energies and cannot be regained by restoring dilation symmetry. Additionally, we observe that the mode with zero propagation velocity corresponds to the volume fraction of the system. Furthermore, the models presented here can undergo phase transitions into the phase characterized as a Mott insulator, breaking both translation and dilation symmetries, in which the zero-propagating mode represents the volume fraction of the system. These findings can be applied to systems like graphene and other 2D materials on a lattice. The analysis also reveals that the description of these systems requires higher derivative terms that correct the motion of fractons, in contrast to the predictions of conventional theories. The theories developed here can also be applied to systems in motion, in which case the description of the effective field theory needs to incorporate the universal coefficients that can be determined through lattice simulations. The research presented here can be expanded to Mott insulators with layering, resulting in the appearance of additional modes with subdimensional propagation, in which case the description of the mode with zero propagation velocity needs to consider the competition between the volume fractions of the system and its layers. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Furthermore, $J_n^T$ is connected to a series of related polynomials, and options are made available for users to calculate these polynomials via an online tool. Leveraging $J_n^T$, we propose a criterion for evaluating whether the volume conjecture holds for a given link, and present computational evidence supporting the application of $J_n^T$ as a method for identifying volume conjecture behavior. Additionally, we explore connections and potential extensions for $J_n^T$. The developments presented in this study build upon prior research described in the accompanying supplementary documents. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding paves the way for more complex searches in proton-lead collisions. Top quark pair production was also shown to be predominantly central, with an average scalar sum of jet momenta of 260 GeV, and the data supported models indicating the w-b pair production process dominates top quark formation. Moreover, the results from this analysis led to the further observation of b quark production in proton-lead collisions. Additionally, b quark production was found to be associated with central scattering processes and characterized by the production of a b quark and a bottom jet with a momentum of 20 GeV. This finding facilitated a key advancement in heavy-flavor analysis for the CMS experiment, enabling searches for other rare processes that are produced in proton-lead collisions. This result was published in the journal Physical Review Letters in its issue 109, 112004 (2007) and a more comprehensive report was later released in the journal Physics Letters B in its issue 695, 103-118 (2011). These studies were carried out using proton-lead data collected at the LHC during 2010 and 2011. A more sophisticated analysis of these data, incorporating additional criteria and refined reconstruction techniques, has led to a further increase in the top quark cross-sectional measurement to 46.8 nanobarns with an 3.1-nanobarn uncertainty, as reported in a paper presented at the 2015 Les Houches Conference on Physics. This result has since been published in the journal Physical Review D in its issue 93, 072012 (2016). These early top quark studies in proton-lead collisions have provided crucial insights for heavy-flavor research and have facilitated more complex searches in proton-lead collisions. As such, they have contributed significantly to the ongoing development of heavy-flavor analysis for the CMS

Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic uniqueness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ik1127/DCAN. For further improvements to temporal action detection, we have also contributed Open Issues for Future Research at https://github.com/ik1127/OpenIssues-FutureResearch-TAD. Leveraging Dual Context Aggregation has the potential to enhance contextual understanding for other video analysis tasks. We hope that our research will serve as a foundation for future work in this domain. Furthermore, we have launched a challenge to gather experts' input on identifying critical open issues and potential applications for DCAN's context aggregation strategy at https://github.com/ik1127/OpenIssues-DCAN. Experts are invited to contribute their expertise in the form of issues on this GitHub page. In return, the contributors will receive a citation in a forthcoming DCAN-related publication and access to a future survey based on their input. The survey's aim is to explore the scalability and generalizability of Dual Context Aggregation across various video analysis tasks. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding signatures in magnetic field readings. Conversely, the detection of 'blobs' captured on a q=4 surface would produce the signature indicative of an outer mode, a variant of PTMs. A key factor supporting these theories is the fact that both inner and outer modes exhibit similar formation dynamics. A collaborative effort between JET and the CSD team has facilitated the development of a three-dimensional model, detailing the formation of a PTM in the post-ELM timeframe. This finding offers novel insights for edge plasma researchers and hints at the intricate relationship between turbulent structures and the formation of palm tree modes. It is hoped that this study will contribute usefully to ongoing discussions on the generation of robust, low-density plasmas in the edge region of fusion devices. A crucial aspect of further research will involve directly observing the structure of a PTM using a high-resolution camera system with a proposed upgrade to the JET tokamak. A key consideration in this study has been the clear communication of complex concepts to a broad audience. To this end, a companion article has been written for the Fusion Sciences and Technology journal, providing a more in-depth examination of these subject matter topics. That article has been entered into the DOIs: 10.1063/1.5111111. A supplementary file containing additional figures and a timeline of key events is available with the supporting information. A related film illustrating these findings is available at: https://doi.org/10.6087

The annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of words is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words with respect to the reference distribution of words.  For renewal times with an algebraic tail, a quenched LDP (conditioned on a typical sequence of letters) was established by Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander, which resulted in a rate function consisting of two components, including the annealed rate function and another component proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by combining the words and randomizing the starting point.  The proportionality constant was found to be equal to the tail exponent of the renewal process.  The purpose of this study is to extend both LDPs to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed by demonstrating that both principles can be applied to sequences of letters satisfying a condition known as summable variation, which provides the necessary condition for both principles to be applicable, while neither of the reference laws involved in the rate functions is independent and identically distributed.  The result of this study is validated by applying it to two specific models, the Eulerian number process and the Pitman-Yor process, both of which yield rate functions with features that are applicable in physics models, such as Ising models, where the observed distribution of words represents the spin configuration and the reference distribution of words represents the ground state.  The property of the Eulerian number process that the observed distribution of words always falls within the reference distribution of words can be interpreted as a phase transition in the Ising model, where the transition occurs when the average spin changes from positive to negative.  The study also extends the result of Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander by demonstrating that the quenched LDP can be applied to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed, which yields a rate function that includes two components, while the proportionality constant remains unchanged, although the study cannot address the ergodic theorem due to the ambiguity of the reference distribution of words. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but the technique offers a valuable framework for assessing and comparing the performance of fuzzers. The implementation details of the evaluation framework are provided as an open-source library. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of the evaluation framework's evaluation results with those obtained from a recent survey on fuzzers is also included. The evaluation framework is available online for download at https://github.com/abdelhamid-m/ModernMutationAnalysis-Fuzzers. Additionally, a supplementary document containing additional information and data points is available to read about at https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13331. Mutation analysis has a rich history that dates back to 1978, and over the years, multiple variations of the technique have been proposed by varying the method for determining reachability in program dependencies. Although the field of program analysis has made significant progress since the introduction of mutation analysis, the basic concept of assessing the ability of program analysis tools to detect artificial flaws remains unchanged. Nonetheless, the reachability problem that underlies mutation analysis has become more complex over time due to the advancement of program optimization techniques, making the evaluation of program analysis tools a more intricate task. As a result, there is a growing need for the development of modern mutation analysis methods that can effectively evaluate the performance of program analysis tools on real-world programs. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods for the first time and provides a comprehensive overview of the history of mutation analysis. Their work demonstrated that these types of games have the capacity for achieving $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ settings. Despite their findings, they left unanswered the question regarding the complexity of obtaining such equilibrium points. Our work contributes a query-efficient conversion from broader classes of games to those defined as Lipschitz games, thereby allowing us to derive a lower-bound restriction for the efficiency of randomized algorithms in finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player games with binary actions and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties, with an exponential relationship between the complexity and the ratio of $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of 'Multi-Lipschitz games' that incorporate distinct Lipschitz rates for each player, followed by a transformation from equilibrium-finding tasks within this broader class to similar tasks within the domain of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, with implications on the sum of individual $\lambda$-Lipschitz parameters. Finally, we establish a lower-bound restriction indicating that deterministic algorithms experience an exponential increase in complexity in finding $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in $n$-player games with multiple action options and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties for particularly restrictive $\epsilon$-value settings, thereby advocating the utilization of randomized algorithms in our previous analysis and further contributing to our methodological simplifications over prior work yielding comparable results. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. The proposed approach achieves superior results when comparing models with the same number of assessments, notably outperforming the standard 5-fold CV approach. The implementation of the proposed method to the GLUE benchmark led to a 0.24% improvement in overall score and the models synthesized an expert's gold standard findings. The technique's potential advantages and potential drawbacks along with future potential research scope are also discussed. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation.
