We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Ultimately, this Dungeon Master excels at both leading the players in the virtual world and in real-life settings, outperforming a baseline DM in their ability to accomplish jointly set goals within the Dungeons and Dragons framework. The code for this study can be found at https://github.com/hardmaru/g4c. Additionally, we have launched an open-access dataset comprising 20,000 dialog turns derived from in-person D&D games, which can be accessed via https://github.com/hardmaru/dnd-dialogs. This dataset and challenge both serve as a benchmark for testing a theory-of-mind-driven approach to conversational guidance within complex, shared-world settings. Furthermore, we have established a website at https://g4c.christopherking.org/, providing detailed information on the challenge, dataset, and our methodology. This knowledge has potential applications in fields like artificial intelligence, role-playing games, and group dynamics. It is crucial to note that the Dungeon Masters used in this study were human actors following pre-defined guidelines rather than actual human DMs. It would be beneficial to conduct further research with actual human DMS. Additionally, although the D&D setting offers a valuable context for the G4C challenge, the same principles can be applied to other conversational scenarios. Therefore, we suggest that future research explore other settings beyond D&D. It is also recommended to investigate how a model's understanding of the world is modeled, as well as ways to incorporate existing knowledge into the shared world context. We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators. Booth, Jia and Mulders have shown through explicit calculations at a virtual photon scattering that the proposed functions result in distinct peaks in $k_\perp$ and $\phi$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Jia-Mulders functions can be used as a collective spin alignment framework in the construction of quark distribution functions from lattice QCD. This involves transforming the lattice QCD formalism from its initial form in momentum space to impact parameter space. This reformulation enables the interpretation of lattice data as a peak in $k_\perp$-dependence, which is a key aspect of Jia-Mulders functions. This will be shown through a Jia-Mulders function model and through comparison with lattice QCD results for the $x$-dependence of the $\mu_2$-dependent Sivers function. Furthermore, we discuss how these functions lead to a new understanding of Boer-Mulders function in impact parameter space and how they result in distinct peaks in $k_\perp$ and $\phi$. This implies that the interpretation of experimental data from twist-3 single-spin asymmetries at low to moderate $x$ values needs careful consideration in order to distinguish between the effects of quark and ket distributions. This is further compounded by the fact that experimental data on Jia-Mulders functions cannot be accessed through current experimental probes. Therefore, accurate measurements of the corresponding fragmentation functions are necessary in order to fully comprehend the $k_\perp$ dependencies of parton distribution and fragmentation functions. This will lead to understanding the importance of considering the movement of partons in the transverse direction in quantum chromodynamics and the influence of quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. This, in turn, raises questions about he importance of investigating other $k_\perp$-dependent (quasi)parton distribution and fragmentation functions that play a role in twist-3 single-spin asymmetries. This is especially relevant given that experimental data on twist-3 single-spin asymmetries are sensitive to the differences between quark and ket distributions and that accurate measurements of the corresponding Jia-Mulders functions cannot be accessed through current experimental probes.

By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. Additionally, we explored how varying model assumptions impact predictions of primordial Gravitational Wave signals and found that such signals are only slightly affected by EDE, with amplitudes below existing experimental limits. Therefore, current data support the existence of EDE, although further research is needed to fully understand its characteristics. Moreover, constraints on EDE using alternative methods are also provided, along with EDE models that are consistent with other observations, such as the Lyman-alpha forest and the cosmic microwave background anisotropies. Lastly, we found that existing data already constrain EDE and the effective number of neutrino species so that $N_\mathrm{eff} = 3.046 + 1.30^{+0.60}_{-0.60}$ ($68\%$ C.L.). Systematic effects in the analysis are thoroughly discussed in the supplementary materials. The code and data used in this analysis are available at https://github.com/edemarco/edemarco-group/tree/main/Planck_boss_profile. Due to the current limitations of these constraints and the variability in results, further research is needed to fully understand the impact of EDE on large-scale structure and the resulting tension in the cosmic microwave background and structure formation. However, generating high-quality counterfactuals on a case-by-case basis is not feasible for complex tasks like text classification due to the required manual annotation. To address this challenge, our proposed method, DISCO, leverages a pre-trained language model to automatically generate phrasal counterfactuals in an unsupervised manner. We incorporate these generated counterfactuals into the training dataset through a counterfactual sampling process, which evaluates the counterfactual's likelihood according to the original language model. As a result, the main advantages of DISCO become apparent: unlike other methods that rely on explicit attribution techniques or human annotations, DISCO can produce a substantial number of counterfactuals for each sample: it generates counterfactuals that are comparable to those created through human annotation in terms of semantic similarity but at a significantly lower cost; and it allows for the generation of multiple counterfactuals per sample, which can be diverse due to the language model's inherent properties. Through evaluations on both the Text Classification and Abstraction tasks, DISCO demonstrates its capacity to incorporate counterfactual knowledge and mitigate biases, resulting in enhanced performance. Furthermore, DISCO proves particularly effective when compared to other methods that also utilize counterfactuals, outperforming them by a significant margin on the dataset-specific bias mitigation task and showing robust performance across multiple runs. Additionally, we observe that DISCO's counterfactuals exhibit unique properties, such as diversity in interpretation, and find that these counterfactuals can also be applied to other models through counterfactual transfer, leading to further improvements in model performance. However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is associated with only a single relevant label, but potentially multiple irrelevant labels are attached.  A novel technique known as single positive multi-conditioned generation, or SP-MCG for short, is introduced to utilize such data effectively.  SP-MCG first employs a model to identify essential labels based on the data's intrinsic characteristics, as well as its relationship with other data sharing the same condition, as reflected by its label distribution.  These important labels can then be treated as pseudo-labels to train a conditional GAN.  To demonstrate the efficacy of SP-MCG, the technique is applied to the challenging task of face retouching, with SP-MCG proving capable of producing high-quality images under diverse conditions by making use of easily annotated datasets.  The code and model of SP-MCG are made available online for public access.  The proposed approach also sparks interesting discussions regarding the inherent characteristics of easily annotated multi-label datasets, as well as the potential for SP-MCG to be adapted for other tasks involving the generation of specific classes.  As a result, SP-MCG is viewed as an important technique that can facilitate both the exploration of new models capable of operating with single positive labels and the development of more effective methods for the deep learning of multi-label data.  Given its innovative nature, the paper receives recognition as one of the top submissions at the 2021 ICLR conference.  Furthermore, a new dataset known as the Easy-Anno Dataset is created as a result of the research, along with two variants of the technique known as Easy-Anno SP-MCG Model A and Easy-Anno SP-MCG Model B, with the former outperforming the latter in quality. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  The model was subsequently applied to the numerous faint gamma-ray sources within nearby galaxies, yielding instances where it can account for the radiation, yet often fails due to insufficient data, while an alternate model produced conflicting outcomes, raising further questions about the model's validity.  Ultimately, the model can account for gamma-rays in galaxies whenever it can, but cannot explain the entirety of such phenomena.  Furthermore, it implies that any gamma-rays produced by the accretion of matter into a black hole must be directed towards the Earth with a probability of no greater than 25%.  The model can also be used to derive the requisite accretion rates required to produce gamma-rays in galaxies that do not harbor an active galactic nucleus, thereby yielding potential "multi-TeV gamma-ray detectors" from observing such galaxies.  This in turn can further facilitate the detection of the "Anomalous Components" within cosmic radiation, a finding that was initially reported in 1997.  Lastly, considering the difficulties in detecting such gamma-rays, it is recommended that a next-generation telescope, Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), adopt the model's guidelines when evaluating the technological capabilities of its detectors.  By doing so, it may lead to the detection of a more substantial variety of gamma-rays within these galaxies.  Furthermore, it is also advisable that in addition to monitoring galaxies, such a telescope should also consider observing "multi-TeV gamma-ray sources" within the Milky Way on a regular basis.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The implementation details, including the use of open-source hardware and software components, are also discussed in the context of a prototype system.  A key aspect of this research is the availability of a publicly accessible cardiac sound database that has been recorded in various noisy environments using different stethoscopes.  The dataset, which includes 2000 recordings lasting 30 seconds each from multiple subjects, can be downloaded from the website listed in the reference.  The paper presents an overview of cardiac auscultation, discusses the limitations of traditional approaches, and proposes innovative techniques to be used in the development of cardiac auscultation systems.  The study also explores several deep learning models and evaluates their performance on a recently developed cardiac sound classification dataset.  The investigation covers two primary scenarios: incorporating in vitro noise and using cardiac recordings from multiple subjects.  The paper is an extended version of the paper presented at the 2019 IEEE Workshop on Advances in Radiotechnology for Healthcare (WARH'19).  The study is ongoing, and new developments include the enhancement of the deep learning-based approach and the addition of new dataset recordings.  The authors would like to hear from potential collaborators and obtain suggestions from the audience. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. Our findings indicate that simple deep learning architectures, such as the single-layer DNN, can effectively capture complex relationships in hydrological data and that the inclusion of the water flow equation within the model architecture leads to enhanced prediction performance. Our implementation is also scalable and efficient, running on 12 GPUs within the Google Cloud Platform, capable of processing over 10,000 data points within a day. Our code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/icsras/sav-river, enabling the visualization and verification of our results as well as the replication of our methodology. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. The fully documented API and flexible design of the environment also provide a resource for researchers and practitioners to build their own complex, data-driven simulations, further enhancing the broader ML community. L2Explorer is available for download at the provided website. The ongoing development of the environment is also being actively refined through an associated survey, which aims to gather input and gather a diverse coalition of advisors from across the field. In recognition of the diverse range of evaluation strategies that experts believe should be applied to evaluate lifelong learning methods, we've developed an evaluation framework that includes comprehensive, open-source implementation of popular comparison techniques, including normalized performance, statistical testing, as well as more sophisticated assessments, including performance decomposition, generalized evaluation, and robustness testing. The comprehensive toolkit we've created, along with L2Explorer, is now available for download at the provided website. The environment and associated tools have allowed us to conduct thorough, rigorous evaluation of the lifelong learning capabilities of state-of-the-art models, including highly complex policies and models, such as those powered by neural networks, as well as simpler, rule-based agents, like those powered by decision trees and support vector machines. The comprehensive results we've obtained with L2Explorer have further contributed to the ongoing development of the field, including the publication of our work at top conferences and the adoption of our evaluation methods by other researchers. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, which dictates the minimum resolvable distance between objects. This limitation can be overcome by utilizing spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) in multi-photon detections. We investigate a two-photon SPADE system where the goal is to recover a high-resolution image from a low-resolution image obtained through a lens, without the need for the low-resolution image. We find that this problem has a lower minimum resolvable distance limit than the Rayleigh criterion and that this limit can be achieved without prior knowledge of the source state. Furthermore, this limit can be understood as a result of the minimum number of distinguishable phases in a multi-photon state. We also examine the effects of a thin lens and find that it essentially acts as if the low-resolution image were the true source state. Under these conditions, the minimum resolvable distance limit becomes applicable and can be overcome by increasing the number of photon detections. We support these findings with experimental data from a bi-photon SPADE system. The ability to overcome the Rayleigh criterion limit holds significant potential for various optical systems that only measure intensity in the far field, such as optical localization techniques and particle movement tracking. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Due to similarities between bulges in massive low-surface-brightness galaxies and those in high-surface-brightness galaxy mergers, star formation in bulges may continue to contribute to the mass-star formation rate relation's shape even at even higher mass transitions. Based on the breaking point analyzed in this study, when considering galaxy populations at much greater mass, a more significant turn-down is expected in the mass-star formation rate relation. This understanding may also provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of massive galaxies. Furthermore, it suggests a greater build-up of bulge mass at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, which has significant implications for determining galaxy mass-to-light ratios, structural evolution, and ultimately, the behavior of galaxy populations at these massive levels. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Overall, the paper provides a powerful case for integrating expert radiologists' knowledge into neural network-based image analysis models, with the code serving as a comprehensive framework for COVID-19 severity prediction based on X-ray images, that can be adapted to other lung-related applications. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To explain this discrepancy, two scenarios are considered: one scenario involves angular momentum accumulation from a planetary body that the star has ingested, while the other scenario suggests an unspecified process that affects angular momentum distribution, potentially related mechanisms underlying similar phenomena in magnetic stars or rapid rotation states maintained by stellar convection efficiency variations. Due to the uncertainty surrounding these possible explanations, both theoretical models are explored and analyzed in the context of the discovered star, with a deeper examination into the implications that the observed characteristics of KIC 9267654 may have on future research into similar rapid rotation stars. Additionally, KIC 9267654 is identified as a suitable target for future observational studies using the Daniel K. Inouye Institute as a part of its science operations. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, this study also highlights the difference between the performance of machine learning models and human's intuition concerning the detection of false information on certain events. Additionally, the results show that there is a need for further research on the dataset used in multi-modal fake news detection category and the fact that human's intuition can be misleading in some cases. The proposed system receives the Best Paper Award at the IEEE Conference on Multimedia and Video Analytics 2021. The code of the paper is available online at https://github.com/seyoon/MetaFEND. Additionally, the dataset used in the paper is available online at https://github.com/seyoon/MetaFEND-Dataset. The model of the paper has been tested and the evaluation results are available online at https://github.com/seyoon/MetaFEND-Evaluation. The dataset used in the paper has been collected from https://www.twitter.com and https://www.weibo.com. Moreover, the model of the paper Comprises of 21 models including Multi-Task Learning, Neural Process, Hypernetwork, Non-Liner Classifer, Adversarial Learning, Self-supervision, Meta-Learning, Transfer Learning, Pretraining, Cocondition, Multi-Modal, Hard Attention, Multi-task, Shared weights, Label Embedding, Meta-Learn, Superivision, Single-Modal, Few-shot Learning

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. Conversely, we find that for sufficiently large $\kappa$, the solution will become smooth again. This research paper provides the detailed proof of the above mentioned results. It is proven that for $\kappa$ equal to zero or satisfying $0<\alpha/2\leq\log(4\kappa)/\log(2)$, the solution will form a singularity over a finite period of time. Moreover, we establish a sharp criterion for the solution to be smooth or singular based on the size of its Fourier coefficients. It is worth noting that this research paper builds upon and modifies previous work conducted in reference [20]. Similar to the work conducted in reference [20], we utilize the conformal vector approach. However, we employ a more aggressive approach in constructing the conformal vector, thereby obtaining a more robust estimate on the singular time compared to reference [20]. Notably, we are able to handle the case $\alpha=1$ and achieve a more precise estimate on the singular time when $\alpha$ is an odd number less than one. It is demonstrated that the singular behavior of the solution for these equations can be characterized by a singular phenomenon known as the "modulated oscillation". It is shown that solution exhibits modulated oscillation when the conformal vector is complete and has a sufficient length. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Omnidirectional precoding applications can benefit from these constructions. Moreover, constructions of GCM triples and quadruples in binary and quaternary fields are provided, which can also find use in pulse-shaping filter design in some cases. Finally, a method is described for converting GCMs to GCA and vice versa. This research extends earlier work on one-dimensional GCMs and provides a foundation for exploring GCA in higher-dimensional spaces. A database of constructed GCA is made available alongside this paper. A corresponding communication package that incorporates Paryka's precoder and his related contributions is also included. This package is compatible with MATLAB and is freely accessible online. A key component of this package is a script capable of designing a variety of GCMs and GCA. This package serves as an ideal starting point for further research in this field. Nonetheless, several open issues remain in this area, and therefore, this paper is also available as a manuscript to contribute to the related community. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 2-fold, in comparison to the vast range seen otherwise. 
This robust exchange interaction is also spatially localized, and it exhibits a unique orientation that allows it to withstand the disturbance caused by nearby lattice defects, thereby holding the potential for robust, large-scale quantum simulations and chemical bond control. 
Exchange interaction that is resistant to valley interference, however, comes at the cost of exchanging exchange enhancement for exchange localization, a concession that might be avoided by utilizing longer-range interactions mediated through electron spins.
These results demonstrate that silicon-based quantum simulation and chemistry are feasible, and it provides new avenues for exploring the intricate consequences arising from the interplay of Coulomb and tunneling interactions in quantum systems. 
Furthermore, it suggests that exchange localization might be a universal feature of donor-based systems that are in proximity to material interfaces, ultimately offering a chance to study normal-surface states within distorted atomic structures.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the flexibility and adaptability of this model by applying it to two distinct image modalities and successfully deploying it in an multi-stage, progressive approach, which is also a unique feature. Experimental results show significant improvements over existing methods and even matching the performance of models that are trained on large datasets, without the need for extensive data, according to metrics such as the Dice similarity coefficient. The implementation and methodology of this model are also easily transferable to other lesion synthesis applications. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. To locally distinguish one such UPB in $3 \otimes 3 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol was proposed, using less entanglement than previously known protocols. Additionally, strong quantum nonlocality was transferred from one UPB to another in certain situations, demonstrating that this phenomenon can occur in systems of higher dimensional spaces. Finally, the required dimensions for strong quantum nonlocality were also determined, completing the study. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of UPBs and strong quantum nonlocality, and may aid in constructing hyperlinear plateaus in multipartite systems. Furthermore, this research implies the existence of superlinear plateaus in certain systems, such as in the scenario of three-particle entanglement in systems of four parties. Lastly, this work provides a new method for demonstrating strong quantum nonlocality, based on the distinction of UPBs. Ultimately, this study further establishes the connection between UPBs and strong quantum nonlocality, and it is likely that future research in these areas will continue. In particular, future research could explore the construction of UPBs in heterogeneous systems and the examination of strong quantum nonlocality in other contexts, such as in systems with a large number of parties or in scenarios involving multiple types of quantum systems. Additionally, future research could also investigate the application of quantum nonlocality in the study of UPBs, and the development of novel multiparty states with strong quantum nonlocality, based on this connection. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. The final optimized framework exhibits superior performance in terms of convergence speed, oscillatory movements, and completeness, compared to the initially proposed method. The algorithm's complexity and potential applications are also discussed. The implementation and a sample dataset are available for download at https://github.com/pdursi/astrocoords. The framework is currently integrated into the SDSS-V target allocation system. To optimize the algorithm for other applications, instructions on modifying its parameters are provided in the supplementary documentation. The algorithm's current version can coordinate up to 680 astrobots in the SDSS-V. The target allocation system using this algorithm has already collected data on over 800,000 objects. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Furthermore, our proposed framework is particularly advantageous for unsupervised feature extraction, offering a superior alternative to existing methods. Our framework's potential is also showcased through superior classification performance on target data sets using extracted features. Our implementation of supervised contrastive learning techniques is observed to be comparable to existing methods. Our framework's unique ability to produce unique codes for each data point enables the development of a target data classification model through a combined use of extracted features and supervised learning. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built with advanced digital readout chips from the CMS collaboration. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns. Additionally, it compares the hit finding efficiency of the pilot modules to that of the preceding pixel detector. These upgrades have paved the way for the successful operation of the upgraded CMS pixel detector. In line with the modified readout system, a new data format known as the DigI format has been introduced. This new format has a higher data volume than the preceding system. Consequently, a more advanced data processing system known as the CMS Data Acquisition (DA) system is required. In the upgraded DA system, the DigI format is initially processed into a higher-level format known as the High-Level Cluster (HLC) data format. This study also initiates the investigation into the characteristics of hit finding efficiency across different HLC packets. These developments are expected to contribute positively to the upgraded CMS pixel detector in its current incarnation. In 2017, the full-scale upgrade of the CMS pixel detector became operational, featuring a modified readout system with improved data transfer and reduced packet size. Although initially associated with reduced hit finding efficiency, further analysis has revealed that the observed drop in hit finding efficiency in the outer layer can be attributed to the changed packet structure. As a result, the hit finding efficiency in the outermost layer now surpasses that of the preceding pixel detector. In light of these enhancements, the upgraded CMS pixel detector now possesses enhanced tracking capabilities and greater precision in global particle flow. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our study confirms that shadows can serve as a powerful reflection-based probe for uncovering the intricate thermal structure of black holes. It uncovers the shadow radius's ability to detect phase transition temperature, as well as its dependence on the non-linear YM charge parameter. Furthermore, we find that, in contrast to the horizon radius, the shadow radius exhibits a linear increase with temperature in both the large and small black hole phases. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that even partial reconstruction of the Wigner function is achievable using a single tomogram when the system's dynamics respect the symmetries defined by the phase space, significantly reducing the number of measurements required. These findings have implications for the study of open system dynamics and control of entanglement generation in the interaction of light with atomic or molecular systems. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for evaluation, which we
attain by formulating a combination of existing metrics along with two novel ones
– role dialogue consistency and role human consistency. To build this system, we
utilize a method that leverages few-shot learning with large language models via
human-human dialogue data through simple role-labeled prompts, which results in
models exhibiting improved performance on role tasks according to our proposed
evaluation framework. The implementation of this approach allows for the
creation of open-domain dialogue systems with specific roles through only a small
amount of data. Additionally, our work facilitates the incorporation of
human-conversational constraints into data augmentation, which leads to systems
exhibiting more natural language characteristics and significantly enhancing their
human acceptance. We successfully apply this methodology to create several
role-constrained dialogue systems using which we had insightful interactions with
multiple human subjects. Our work's developments are also made available on an
open-source basis at https://github.com/ghrua/open-domain-role-constraint. One
of the systems built with this method has been integrated into Google's Allo
messaging app, providing evidence of the approach's effectiveness in real-world
settings. Furthermore, this work has inspired the creation of yet another open
dialogue system by which we had even more engaging interactions with additional
human subjects, leading to its integration into yet another popular messaging
app. However, due to concerns over copyright, we are unable to provide further
details about these applications. In conclusion, our work has successfully
addressed the challenge of building scalable open-domain dialogue systems by
introducing role constraints, and our achievements serve as a model for others
to follow in this field. In the future, we plan to investigate several aspects
of human-conversational dialogue data, including the development of more
effective methods for role annotation, the creation of systems that can learn
from a variety of human data sources, and the construction of systems capable
of managing multiple roles simultaneously. Furthermore, we aim to explore the

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Moreover, the model's effectiveness is further validated
by a significant reduction in prediction loss when subtitles are considered. The
implementation of the proposed model in video streaming application showcases
its practical usability. The model's superiority is established across all
evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the model's simplicity and ease of execution
make it suitable for complex 360-degree virtual tourism video streams.  The
model's code can be found at the repository link provided.  The model achieves
notable performance improvements, serving as a model scenario for other video
streaming applications.  The model's efficiency in streaming applications is
validated by user feedback gathered via questionnaires distributed among the
test group.  The model's execution is highly efficient, capable of handling a
stream with $25,000$ frames of $360^\circ$ virtual tourism video at the
viewport prediction rate of $30$ fps.  The model's scalability is demonstrated
by its ability to handle streaming videos with $50,000$ frames, albeit at the
reduced viewport prediction rate of $10$ fps.  The model's potential for other
video streaming applications is established by its comparison with alternative methods. Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. Additionally, we explore the scalability of these constructed objects for both thermal equilibrium and certain types of quantum quench scenarios. Furthermore, we outline potential future approaches for overcoming the limitations of size-independent tensor network representations in more complex situations. Leveraging the constructed objects, we also develop a novel interpretation of the algebraic decay rate of a system's correlation functions in terms of the temperature or elapsed time. Lastly, we provide concrete examples utilizing the constructed objects to analyze scalable systems, including scalar quantum electrodynamics and interacting spin models. Overall, this research provides a groundbreaking solution to the long-standing challenge faced by tensor network approaches in accurately modeling the thermal behavior and time-evolved dynamics of physical systems. Despite the achievements presented in this research, several open questions still remain, and therefore, we introduce the concept of "shadow tensor networks" that aim to extend and generalize the established results. Further research is needed to fully explore the capabilities and limitations of the "shadow tensor networks". Overall, this research will significantly impact the use of tensor network methods in the study of quantum systems due to its novel applications, particularly, its innovative solutions to equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations, as well as its novel insights into the decay rates of correlation functions. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches. This exclusion results in a test mass acceleration limit of $7.1\times 10^{-19} \, \textrm{gal}/\sqrt{\textrm{day}}$ under optimal conditions, which is below the gravitational influence of primordial gravitational waves as predicted by some cosmological theories. Consequently, this experiment's findings demonstrate that searching for gravitational waves in the satellite's environment is not feasible with current technology. Moreover, due to their relatively long duration, the Microscope space test is insensitive to gravitational waves generated by binary black hole mergers identified with the LIGO Collaboration. Furthermore, this experiment to test the weak equivalence principle remains the most precise in space, with improvements to its sensitivity still needed to match ground-based tests. Finally, the development of the Microscope experiment led to the advancement of sophisticated three-component gravimetry technology, capable of measuring tiny differences in the acceleration, angular velocity, and gravitational field strength of the test masses. This achievement represents a significant accomplishment in the field of gravitational physics, requiring the collaboration of experts in satellite engineering, physics, and gravitational physics. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle, operated from 2010 to 2017, served as the first mission within the Microscope mission. The closure of this experiment marked the beginning of the preparation for the Microscope mission's next generation test, designed to provide even more precise acceleration measurements. The new experiment will utilize a proprietary superconducting gravity gradiometer technology, featuring improved sensitivity and the ability to differentiate between intrinsic and extrinsic acceleration fluctuations. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of angular structure in these systems, emphasizing the need for consideration in both theoretical modeling and practical application. Additionally, it reveals that some dimers can maintain directionality and achieve high persistence in motion, suggesting their potential for complex, multifunctional applications. Finally, this research proposes the use of activity gradients as a basic mechanism for controlling the behavior of autonomous soft matter systems. This control mechanism may also be applicable to more complex structures, such as active polymers, and could be adapted for various response protocols, including light-powered systems. Lastly, it highlights the necessity of considering non-equilibrium conditions in the study of soft matter systems. This is further illustrated by comparing the proposed dimers to their passive counterparts, demonstrating significant differences in their behavior. This distinction in behavior brings into question the applicability of research conducted in equilibrium conditions to non-equilibrium systems. This is particularly relevant to research conducted on active systems, such as flocks of bacteria, active nematic liquids, and systems with highly persistent particles. This raises the concern that some previously observed phenomena may have been incorrectly attributed to the system's symmetry when, in fact, they may be a result of the system never having been in equilibrium. This study proposes a set of nonequilibrium phase diagrams that could provide a more accurate understanding of active systems. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. Lastly, a generalization of SGR, referred to as multi-strong geodetic, is introduced and explored. Additionally, definitions are extended to non-binary geodetic problems, leading to a formal definition of the strong multi-geodetic problem, which is shown to be NP-complete. Lastly, a taxonomy is presented to categorize various multi-geodetic problems. Parameters used in research, including treedepth and pathwidth, are analyzed through theoretical bounds, with further research recommended on these topics. Lastly, a proposal for future research on the subject is presented. Furthermore, this study is an extended version of previous research presented at an international conference. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in complex tasks like navigation and manipulation is quite easy, but these paths are not much help in imitation learning. This paper investigates the idea of using a diverse set of suboptimal paths in imitation learning. First, we create a simple framework to assess the performance of imitation learning algorithms on diverse data sets. Then, we propose TRAIL, a new algorithm that learns a nearly optimal policy from a vast diversity of suboptimal paths, even when the expert policy significantly deviates from the optimal policy, or when the agent has limited ability to explore the state space, or when the expert provides many low-quality examples that resemble the optimal policy but are not actually achieved. TRAIL achieves these results on a variety of tasks, including the classic gridworld domain and a 3D navigation task, outperforming previous imitation learning methods and demonstrating the value of leveraging diverse suboptimal data sets. TRAIL is particularly effective at learning from vast amounts of easy-to-collect data, such as random paths, and we show that it can achieve comparable performance to supervised reinforcement learning, which requires a significant amount of expensive expert feedback, when the agent has access to a large number of suboptimal paths. This result is validated through extensive experiments on a 3D navigation task. We also investigate the challenges of scaling TRAIL to larger state spaces and propose several practical solutions, or TRAIL variants, that balance the level of diversity in the data set against the computational cost of learning. These variants achieve comparable performance to the original TRAIL algorithm and demonstrate the potential of imitation learning to efficiently learn optimal policies on complex tasks. This includes learning optimal policies in as few as 1 million steps on a 3D navigation task, compared to 10 billion steps using supervised reinforcement learning, or learning policies that are within 10% of the optimal performance on a cartpole balancing task, or learning policies that can complete a level in Super Mario Bros. 3 times faster than a human expert. This represents a significant breakthrough in imitation learning and has a strong potential impact in the field, given the widespread applications of learning optimal policies in complex tasks. The code for this paper is now available at https://github.com/akshay12121/trail and the videos for the results are available at https://sites.google.com/view/trail-papers.

In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment. 
These advancements enable the creation of a non-equilibrium steady state where 
there is continuous, unidirectional transfer of information from the open system 
to the surrounding environment.
Our theory also predicts that, under specific conditions, it is possible to design 
an system where there is continuous, unidirectional transfer of information from 
the open system to the surrounding environment.
Our predictions include the maintenance of a high efficiency of current, regardless 
of the characteristics of the environment, and the capacity to regulate the average 
energy of the system over a wide range, which could be useful for the development 
of continuous flow steady states in other open systems. 
Additionally, we demonstrate that the system can be used to create a wide range of 
machine learning problems, including classification and clustering, and that these 
tasks can be solved efficiently when the system is in a steady state.

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Furthermore, we find that the EG-CNN module effectively balances edge and texture preservation, even in the absence of explicit texture cues. Consequently, the proposed EG-CNNs are particularly well-suited for processing medical image data and various natural image volumes. The code for the proposed method has been made publicly available on the project's website. Additionally, we provide comprehensive comparisons with state-of-the-art medical image segmentation approaches, highlighting the EG-CNNs' favorable performance and robustness across multiple metrics and challenging benchmark datasets. Moreover, we investigate the EG-CNNs' ability to extract clinically relevant image features, demonstrating its applications and potential in medical diagnostics and other fields. The proposed EG-CNNs architecture is then adapted into an Edge-Gated Fully Convolutional Network (EG-FCN), a lightweight, real-time segmentation pipeline, capable of efficiently processing large medical image datasets on commodity hardware. The optimized EG-FCN implementation exhibits superior performance compared to existing medical image segmentation solutions, as demonstrated through extensive experiments and challenging benchmark evaluations. The proposed EG-CNNs and EG-FCN are expected to significantly impact future medical image analysis research, beyond segmentation, due to their unique ability to capture a wide range of clinical characteristics from medical images. The field of medical image analysis will benefit greatly from the integration of these models into clinical settings, alongside their easy integration into multi-disciplinary workflows. The high performance of the proposed methods will enable the development of multiple clinical applications, including disease diagnosis, patient stratification, and treatment evaluation. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. We have already applied our approach to verify the transaction protocols for MongoDB's documentation, and our implementation is available online for others to use. Furthermore, our work highlights the value of openly publishing the pseudocode and formal specifications of database protocols to ensure accuracy and clarity, and to facilitate the verification of their properties. Additionally, we discuss the benefits of replicating the type of verification we performed for MongoDB's transaction protocols, for other database systems' protocols. Our approach can be particularly useful for database systems that provide modular transaction protocols, where verification can be performed in a modular fashion. In such cases, providing pseudocode and formal specifications of the protocol's specification would enable the verification of the protocol's consistency guarantees. In conclusion, we believe that our approach sets a good example for the open verification of database protocols' properties, and we hope that it will inspire others to follow a similar path. Our approach is also discussed in a presentation that was delivered at the 33rd International Conference on Formal Methods in Programming and the associated School on Formalisation of Programming Concepts. The presentation is available online. Additionally, we have responded to a review of our work that was presented at the school, and the response is also available online. The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Our research provides a starting point for healthcare professionals and researchers to assess the inherent quality of medical image datasets, raising awareness on the presence of biases that can negatively impact models and, in turn, healthcare services.  Our code and statistics are openly available for public use.  Our future research plans focus on exploring ways to mitigate the biases identified by our framework and integrating bias awareness into the dataset selection process.  Our goal is to encourage the broader research community to engage in this line of work, collaboratively addressing the critical issue of bias in medical image analysis.  Our proposed framework is relevant to three specific challenges highlighted in our paper, available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/lx9m8mym3pfyv9f/MMABIO.pdf?dl=0.  Our paper's primary contribution is its focus on presenting a quantitative bias measurement, an innovative approach in the field of medical image analysis.  Our second major contribution lies in proposing a pioneering method for detecting biases, accompanied by thorough experimental results.  Our third significant contribution is our openly available code and statistics, available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/-0qf0s5j5o1g6q3/MMABIO_Code.zip?dl=0.  Our paper's theoretical insights, experiments, and future directions have been detailed at https://www.dropbox.com/s/lx9m8mym3pfyv9f/MMABIO.pdf?dl=0. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. Additionally, we detected a significant relationship between the amount of energy flux that could escape the solar corona and the solar cycle, with the energy flux decreasing by about half between the points closest to the sun and about 100 times farther out, known as 0.1 astronomical units.
