Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. We employ Domain-Specific Batch Normalization to normalize anatomical feature maps from the two domains separately, introduce a cross-domain contrastive learning approach to promote extracting domain-invariant features, and integrate these into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework that leverages unlabeled target domain images and incorporates prediction consistency constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the CS-CADA's ability to solve the complex cross-anatomy domain shift issue, resulting in the accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-ray images, aided by retinal vessel images, and cardiac MR images, aided by fundus images, with only a limited number of target domain annotations. Comparisons with alternative approaches validate the superiority of our method. The project's code is available at https://github.com/xbonifay/CS-CADA.

The foundation of contemporary supergravity, often referred to as the '1.5 order trick', has been extensively analyzed in a simplified theoretical framework based on the Wess-Zumino theory. A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all contexts. Although it appears that the associated algebra is closed, a detailed examination in a simplified setting reveals the presence of a non-nilpotent BRS operator generated by the 1.5 order formalism. Consequently, this is also applicable to supergravity, suggesting the necessity of formulating revised nilpotent transformations to salvage the 1.5 order formalism. Two potential alternatives have been proposed, along with an explanation of their implications. Furthermore, we propose a nilpotent transformation generated by the 1.5 order formalism, which can be achieved by combining the closure generators and reinforcing the supersymmetry non-central charge. This resulting transformation yields a closed algebra and generates the off-shell supergravity multiplex. Additionally, we identify a connection between the 1.5 order formalism and the super-descent, which enables the reconstruction of superfields from components. Building upon this understanding, we develop a nilpotent transformation for the superconformal tensor multiplet. Finally, we observe that the 1.5 order formalism can be applied in theories where the central supersymmetry non-compactified is compactified on a circle, resulting in the presence of a non-nilpotent BRS operator generated by the 1.5 order formalism. Nevertheless, we propose that this phenomenon arises from the improper application of the super-descent in such settings, which would need further exploration. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This is different from the traditional approach, where the angular velocity is treated as a global, uniform property of the star. Instead, we solve for the angular velocity in each fluid element through the use of an iterative algorithm. This leads to more precise and adaptable solutions, especially in stars with complex rotation patterns.

The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the development of an innovative multi-stage system combining techniques like named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention.

We utilized the N2C2 Shared Task data consisting of 4480 annotated sections on twelve different social determinants of health sourced from MIMIC-III and University of Washington Harborview Medical Centers to test our proposed system. Given the challenge posed by entities that overlap with each other, our team designed a unique marker-based model, which we incorporated into the multi-stage system. 

In our experiments, our proposed system consistently demonstrated exceptional performance by achieving better overall Micro-F1 score and outshining existing state-of-the-art models when handling the critical issue of overlapping entities.

Ultimately, our study successfully validated the potential of the proposed system to effectively identify and extract vital social determinants of health information from clinical notes, a crucial development with the potential to enhance clinical care and monitoring. However, there are concerns regarding error propagation, necessitating future research to further optimize entity extraction, particularly when encountering entities with complex meaning and a scarcity of available data. Additionally, there are questions regarding how to seamlessly integrate this technology into existing clinical workflows and ensure the robust handling of sensitive information as required by HIPAA. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. This research targets resolving secrecy concerns for nonorthogonal multiple access users by introducing an alternative decoding order method. First, we mathematically quantify the total possible decoding order options. We then propose an effective decoding order approach that guarantees positive secrecy rates for each user and, through computation, determine the feasible secure decoding order quantities. To minimize complexity in determining the best secure decoding order, we also present an efficient yet suboptimal solution strategy. Notably, the proposed suboptimal solution achieves around 137% improvement in performance over a relevant benchmark solution. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to validate the proposed approaches. Introduction: Over the recent past, considerable growth has been observed in mobile data usage, which has resulted in rising demands for next-generation wireless communications to support high-speed data transfer. As a key technology within these communications systems, NOMA is gaining attention due to its capacity to serve a wide range of users with varying channel conditions. Nevertheless, one significant drawback of existing NOMA implementations is the requirement for users to adhere to a specific decoding order, which is often determined based on the relative strength of their signal. If users fail to cooperate in this regard, it becomes possible for an adversary to exploit this vulnerability and compromise the entire system. As a result, there is a pressing need to investigate methods of securing communications systems equipped with untrusted users. Existing research studies primarily focus on developing solutions tailored to specific system configurations, such as conventional multiple-access technologies or CR-based applications. In contrast, this research seeks to explore the fundamental characteristics of decoding order in NOMA systems. A key aspect of our investigation involves defining the general form of feasible decoding order sequences. We propose an efficient approach for generating a crucial subset of secure decoding order sequences. Notably, the proposed approach yields results that are on average 137% better than existing alternatives. Finally, our findings are further validated through numerical simulations. The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence. Further analysis on their residual spectra in the 1-10 keV range revealed that it doesn't conform to a single specific shape, which led us to adopt a model consisting of an power-law, a blackbody and an iron emission line to describe their spectral characteristics more accurately. When controlling for the impact of accretion rate and column density, we found that asynchronous polars still displayed a significantly more intense hard component, but only when their soft component was significantly weaker than average. This effect, however, could also be influenced by the greater prevalence of accretion rate anomalies among asynchronous polars. Lastly, we observed that the detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray surveys is likely influenced by their spectral characteristics rather than any intrinsic disparity in their soft X-ray emission patterns. Ultimately, the insufficient size of our sample set means that our primary discovery shouldn't be considered significant yet, and future studies should prioritize accurately determining the spectral characteristics of the standard polar population and conducting a similar analysis on the brighter sub-set of non-asynchronous polars. Additionally, researchers should consider investigating the relationship between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its thermal pulse history. Systematic studies of polars using next-generation large-area X-ray detectors will be crucial in addressing these theories and validating our research. Until then, the unique nature of asynchronous polars will remain a topic that warrants further study and analysis. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  The Dragon infrared dark cloud provides a valuable testing ground for these concepts due to its relatively isolated and undisturbed location, free from the impact of external factors that could influence the evolution of its member cores.  Thus, it offers a valuable opportunity to examine the relationship between the mass of these cores and the formation of massive star formation.  In addition, a comparison with the Perseus molecular cloud, characterized by its actively forming protostars and ongoing star formation, reveals a striking contrast in core mass distributions.  The mass distribution of cores within the Dragon infrared dark cloud follows a double-slope pattern as predicted by the global star formation theory, with a distinct break occurring at a core mass of approximately 7-10 times the mass of the sun.  In contrast, the continuum cores from the Perseus molecular cloud exhibit a single-slope distribution with no visible break, reflecting the difference in the spatial scale of these two molecular clouds.  While the Dragon infrared dark cloud covers only 0.45 square degrees on the sky, the Perseus molecular cloud covers approximately 49 square degrees.  As a result, the analysis of cores within the Dragon infrared dark cloud can be considered a more local and distinct population, free from the superposition of multiple forming star clusters that can be observed within the Perseus molecular cloud.  Therefore, research on the continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud offers a unique chance to study massive star formation in a relatively isolated molecular cloud.  It is worth noting that the current understanding of the relationship between the mass of these cores and the formation of massive star formation, based on the analysis of molecular line observations, may need to be re-examined in light of the findings presented in this study. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data. Our research is centered on classifying aerial LiDAR data, but the developed approach can be applied to other classification scenarios involving LiDAR data as well. Our implementation is built on top of the Open3D framework, but our findings are relevant to other LiDAR processing frameworks as well. We hope this research to be a foundation for further exploration and expansion of the topic in future editions. Due to the continually evolving nature of both LiDAR technology and machine learning, we intend for this evaluation to serve as a starting point for subsequent studies. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. As a result, one-step recurrences become achievable, enabling the development of novel applications, particularly in connection with spherical random fields, appearing in stochastic modeling, differential equations, and harmonic analysis. The developed techniques are further illustrated by constructing a sample process with a defined non-stationary covariance operator. The resulting process is utilized to solve a specified class of differential equations, demonstrating the usefulness of the proposed approach. The proposed method is also shown to facilitate derivative representation, addressing the challenge of deriving existing results through the proposed framework. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. We have also observed the transfer of stresses to specific locations within the foam cell and the resulting breakage of soap films. These findings have important implications for the better understanding of flow behavior in complex liquids. Additionally, we have shown that both the "leverage rule" and our tribo-assembly model can be applied not just to dry liquid foams but also, with some modifications, to other complex liquids with interacting interfaces. Nonetheless, the issue of liquid release from these interfaces needs to be addressed differently in these other complex liquids. In the case of dry liquid foams, the "leverage rule" and our tribo-assembly model highlight the crucial role that surface tension plays in stress transfer and discuss the implications of this for the broader category of complex liquids known as suspensions of soft particles. These findings have significant implications for both the scientific theory and the real-world applications of these types of complex liquids. In terms of its scientific contributions, this research provides a deeper understanding of flow behavior in complex liquids and also reveals the importance of surface roughness in determining friction modes. Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. Despite initial hopes for widespread adoption through a universal grid platform, its integration was hindered by complexities. Instead, we identify key factors that facilitated the successful embedding of grid computing in operating systems and applications, focusing on a translational approach involving loose coupling between high-performance computing and applications. This led to the widespread use of grid computing in various domains, as illustrated through case studies of parallel computing, distributed computing, and virtual laboratories. Furthermore, we propose a design framework for translating computer science concepts, drawing on experiences with grid computing. However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, enables them to be utilized within settings that include mini-batch and non-conjugate applications, making them more suitable for practical applications and easier to integrate within broader learning architectures. This research proposes the GMAT\'ern kernel, a novel graph kernel, and shows its effectiveness through experiments on multiple datasets, demonstrating its potential as a powerful tool for graph-related learning tasks. While models incorporating prior smoothness assumptions have proven invaluable in both Euclidean and non-Euclidean spaces, their limitations become more pronounced as graphs become more complex, prompting this research to introduce a new approach. This study adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes, enabling them to handle graphs by utilizing the shortest path metric, specifically the maximum a posteriori estimate for the graph Mat\'ern Gaussian process, which results in an efficient and scalable algorithm. This research addresses several significant challenges in the application of Gaussian processes to graphs, ultimately contributing a novel model that can learn complex graph data. This study demonstrates the benefits of graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes by comparing them to existing models, revealing that they outperform them by a significant margin on multiple datasets, showcasing the effectiveness of graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes as powerful models for graph regression and classification. This research also explores the model's capabilities in modeling real-world graphs, examining various aspects of its behavior, and provides evidence that graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes can learn complex graph data by leveraging multiple underlying features, ultimately leading to several potential applications and future research directions. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the model's properties and its performance in comparison to alternative approaches, as well as a detailed exploration of its behavior and potential, culminating in a clear roadmap for its future development. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall coverage rate of up to 75.5% of all road segments with 97.2% of those implicitly covered, alongside notable reliability enhancements with an increase of at least 16.5% in reliable data collection compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, notable time-saving opportunities of around 13.4% can be achieved through implicit inferences, presenting ample scope for further optimization of urban road management systems with potential applications across multiple domains. Additionally, the scalability and generalizability of this approach are demonstrated through replication of methodology on data from San Francisco and Chicago. With the widespread adoption of mobile sensing technologies and increasingly complex urban transportation networks, the developed approach provides a viable solution for optimizing the monitoring of urban roads, enabling better management and maintenance of these critical infrastructure systems. With sufficient collaboration between transportation agencies and ridesharing companies, this approach holds great potential for replicating results in various settings. In light of numerous benefits derived from mobile sensing and data-driven analysis, the focus should shift towards addressing existing reliability issues and fully leveraging the vast amounts of data collected with enough participation rates, paving the way for a more efficient, safe, and adaptable urban transportation network. In the study's latter stages, the concept of implicit data is introduced, along with a novel algorithm for its validation, before the proposal of an enhanced version of the model that incorporates reliability metrics, followed by real-data testing and a useful solution identified through research, albeit outside the scope of New York City

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, we found that the most sensitive experiment to such neutrino or dark matter energies would be the Belle II detector at the KEKB electron-positron collider, with the ability to test J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter at the 5σ level by the end of its current data collection period. We anticipate this to significantly impact future dark matter research. Additionally, we determined that combining Belle II's J/ψ data with other experiments, particularly those involving muon anomalous magnetic moment measurements and Higgs boson searches at the Large Hadron Collider, would provide further insight into these light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter scenarios. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience. Furthermore, the package Rfssa, also presented here, is a versatile tool designed to facilitate general functional time series analysis, encompassing MFSSA among its components. The temperature data and vegetation data are included as supplementary datasets in the package. The temperature data specifically are made available through the Rfssa's temperature function, providing access to intraday temperature curves from 448 stations across China, as reported by the National Climate Center, with each station possessing 29 years of daily data. The vegetation data, derived from the Global Land Surface Satellite (GLASS), offer 27 years of imagery covering the entire Chinese territory, with approximately 300-400 individual 30km*30km land units observable in each year. A vignette for the Rfssa package is also included, serving as a comprehensive guide on how to use the package for its intended purposes. The temperature and vegetation applications are thoroughly detailed within the vignette. Additionally, the package's installation, loading, and general functionality are explicitly illustrated through the creation of a step-by-step instruction guide. Furthermore, the package's Rfssa function is compared to alternative approaches, including functional principal component analysis (FPCA). The comparison with FPCA is performed in an empirical setting, with results showing that the package's primary function, Rfssa, provides superior results compared to FPCA in terms of extrapolation. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As a result, scores are often dictated by these phrases alone, rendering the model over-stable and ineffective. Interestingly, our study discovered a stark contrast between this outcome and that of other probing studies examining how well these types of pre-trained models grasp more subtle linguistic aspects such as syntax, morphology, and parts-of-speech. Additionally, we identified a further issue: the autoscoring models developed biases towards the data used during training. Consequently, we propose two potential remedies for addressing these concerns: 1) scoring models with reduced complexity (such as linear models) that are less likely to develop unnecessary complexities, and 2) robustness testing as a mandatory validation step to guarantee the stability and reliability of the autoscoring models before deploying them in production environments. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative evaluation framework that incorporates a range of quantitative metrics in addition to qualitative assessments, providing a holistic evaluation approach that encompasses both reliable performance and sensitive analysis. This framework is applicable to a broad range of automated scoring applications. Additionally, we open-source the autoscoring models, data, and evaluation metrics used in this study in the interests of advancing the field. Finally, we highlight the broader implications of these findings for the secure deployment of machine learning models in other domains. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies. Additionally, directional stability for the model's periodic solutions is assessed through the application of a theoretical skew-product approach and numerical simulations. Parameters representing the model's components, including its global stability, have been estimated through a novel approach involving data from various sources, which is also used to develop policy recommendations for the model's components. These recommendations are then validated through numerical simulations conducted across multiple parameter settings. A key component of the model is the Eirich function, which is replaced by a piecewise linear function for nematode population modeling, allowing for discontinuous behavior and thus more accurately capturing the effects of over-population. A key advantage of this model is its ability to manage pest populations through the suppression of their growth, achieving zero pest control when the model's components are set to their optimal values. Furthermore, the model's stability and stability switches provide critical insights for the design of advanced pest control systems, enabling the implementation of control strategies that adapt to changing environmental conditions and thus contributing to a more sustainable and efficient pest management system. Logical extensions to this model are also proposed, focusing on incorporating the effects of external pest populations and competitive nematode species, as well as the application of chemical pesticides, to further enhance its practical usability. Furthermore, the model's potential usability in the development of pest control devices, specifically nematode-releasing robot systems, is also explored. A key consideration in the design of these systems is the implementation of a feedback control mechanism that adapts to changing environmental conditions, and the model's recommendations for its components can be integrated into a controller design, providing a foundation for the development of more advanced pest control systems. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers developed a novel 2D nucleus detection network called W-Net, which is comprised of two stages to segregate nucleus regions and extract distinct feature information from both the input image and a preliminary detection mask. The system also includes a precision-guided strategy that encourages the model to prioritize difficult sample cases during training, with positive results showing W-Net outperforming existing competition baselines and demonstrating robust performance on unsampled test cases. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenHongXing/W-Net. Additionally, pre-trained models and evaluation tools can be found at https://github.com/ChenHongXing/W-Net/tree/main/tools. Furthermore, researchers with relevant expertise are invited to join the Nucleus Detection Challenge (https://www.chenjingliu.com/nucleus-detection-challenge/) to compare their methods against state-of-the-art W-Net approaches. For research purposes only, the challenge will provide access to previously unpublished cancer datasets available at https://www.chenjingliu.com/nucleus-detection-challenge/dataset/. Lastly, due to the diverse nature of medical imaging, researchers are encouraged to test W-Net on various other cancer datasets with distinct characteristics. For instance, researchers have successfully applied modifications to the network, resulting in successful nucleus segmentation within colon, lung, breast, and prostate tissue types. However, further research is needed to thoroughly evaluate the network's performance across a wide range of medical imaging applications. Nonetheless, when compared to state-of-the-art universe mapping approaches like Universal Cross-Modality Detectors (UCD) and Universal Adapters (UA), W-Net demonstrated superior nucleus detection accuracy within histopathological images. For instance, when tested on the HNDataset, W-Net outperformed UCD and UA by achieving a gap of 8.24% and 12.04% in terms of detection accuracy, respectively. Similarly, when tested on the MBDataset, W-Net also demonstrated better performance compared to UCD and UA, resulting in a gap of 10.51% and 13.46% in terms of detection accuracy, respectively. In this study, we examine whether an L^n(G) graph possesses a hamiltonian path, and offer a definition for G to achieve this condition. Additionally, we apply this definition to set multiple upper limits for a graph's hamiltonian path index. Furthermore, we establish relationships between graph parameters like their trace, chromatic number, and minimum degree, which helps in identifying subclasses of graphs that exhibit the desired properties. Finally, we present an open problem and suggestions for future research. In particular, we propose finding whether an L^n(G) graph can have a hamiltonian cycle when G is a cycle or a complete graph. Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of computational processing. This acceleration could be applied across a wide range of reinforcement learning algorithms. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. Additionally, detailed instructions on implementing HELMHOLTZ in an automated manner with Mini-Michelson are provided, along with a demonstration of the efficacy of this approach with a real-world contract deployment. Furthermore, the source code of HELMHOLTZ and its specifications have been made publicly available for further development and integration with the Michelson Editor Toolkit. In contrast to other verification tools that rely on dynamic checks or interprocedural analysis and employ a purely symbolic semantics, HELMHOLTZ employs a combination of static and symbolic semantics to verify the correctness of Michelson programs at once. Consequently, this approach results in a more compact and readable verification proof in comparison to other verification tools. In this article, the focus is on the design and implementation of HELMHOLTZ, with an additional discussion on the integration of refinement types with the Michelson type system and the challenges encountered in developing a static verification tool for smart contracts. Furthermore, future enhancements to HELMHOLTZ are also outlined, including the exploration of liquid refinement types and the development of an interface for user-defined specifications. In the context of static verification tools, the choice of programming language and verification tools used is also disclosed, along with the rationale behind the design and implementation of HELMHOLTZ, with an emphasis on the lessons learned that can be applied to the development of similar verification tools. In conclusion, the potential of static verification tools to enhance the reliability and security of smart contracts is demonstrated, with a call to the Tezos community to collaborate on the integration of refinement types with the Michelson type system and the development of a static verification tool for Tezos smart contracts. In response to the growing demand for static verification tools, the scope of this project is also expanded to include the development of a static verifier for Michelson contracts, with a focus on contract

This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This combined approach yields novel pathways for verifying the correctness of algorithms and identifying new classes of algorithms that can be correctly implemented. This duality between logical pseudocodes and natural deduction/natural generalization also facilitates a new algorithm design method, where algorithms are developed at the logical pseudocodes level and then systematically translated into efficient imperative codes. This paper explores the design and application of logical pseudocodes, featuring an example of correctly implementing an algorithm through this method. This approach holds broader implications for the relationship between programming and logic. Additionally, we discuss the potential for extending logical pseudocodes to address additional programming constructs, such as concurrency and exceptions. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. We explore the associated properties of these probabilities, as well as their connections to the principles of majorization and the related phenomenon of 'weakly cyclic' data sets. Our findings can be verified using an available public repository. Our work provides a theoretical framework for further 'cyclic' related research. Our analysis may offer insights into real-world scenarios, such as the interpretation of empirical data or the design of simulation tools. In addition, our results can be applied to the generation of 'cyclic' scenarios in a variety of fields, such as economics, politics, and biology. Our research may also provide a basis for exploring new areas, such as the development of specialized statistical tests or the creation of educational tools to promote critical thinking. Our work can serve as a starting point for further investigation into real-world applications of 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' phenomena. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters. Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task

performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating

scenarios. The code for our experiments is openly accessible on GitHub. By
examineing the results and the associated policy representations, we deduce that
the tendency of model-based multi-task reinforcement learning to perform worse
when shared dynamics models are used may arise due to an increased risk of
catastrophic interference among task-specific action probabilities. In turn, this
means that modular networks offering distinct sub-representations for each task
can be viewed as a form of multi-task reinforcement learning where the tasks
are highly similar, with the added benefit of facilitating easy policy
transfer. Ultimately, our research suggests that the benefits of modular networks

reinforcement learning settings as well. We propose the term "catastrophic
interference" to describe this phenomenon and argue that modular networks are
an effective solution to prevent it. In conclusion, our study highlights the
importance of scrutinizing the underlying representation learned by shared models
in multi-task reinforcement learning settings, with a view to informing the
development of more efficient and effective multi-task reinforcement learning

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce scintillation patterns at different times and under specific radio frequency conditions. While the screens' distances cannot be determined directly, their positions and movements within the sky plane were determined, ranging from 0.76 to 21.29 degrees in right ascension. Additionally, two screens were found to be located in the Earth's vicinity, one moving rapidly across the line of sight to the pulsar and interacting with screens in the line of sight, producing scintillation patterns and potential disruptions in signal reception, consistent with reported anomalies in pulsar data. These findings highlight the utility of scintillation patterns in mapping the local interstellar medium and understanding how it affects observations of distant astronomical sources. Furthermore, they emphasize the importance of continuing pulsar observations, providing valuable data for studying the line of sight and identifying potential anomalies, in addition to contributing to general astronomical research goals. These results demonstrate that by extensively recording dynamic spectra from bright pulsars, a significant amount of useful information about the interstellar medium can be obtained, alongside accurate recovery of previously known screens and their moving patterns. This study incorporates data from the single-dish receiver used at Arecibo, which provides wide bandwidth and recording capabilities, enabling the detailed analysis of data that cannot be processed from other telescopes. Nonetheless, with the advent of new radio telescopes like FAST and their significantly enhanced sensitivity, it is crucial to reconsider and revise previous studies based on data from these newer facilities. Nonetheless, the findings presented in this paper remain relevant and provide valuable insights into the physics of the interstellar medium. Furthermore, as pulsar timing arrays for gravitational wave detection are being constructed, understanding scintillation screens and their moving patterns is becoming increasingly important, along with the potential for bias introduction when analyzing data sets. Consequently, this study recommends considering the effects of scintillation screens and their movements when analyzing data and processing research goals, in addition to continuing observations of pulsar variability, and provides stakeholders with relevant findings and recommendations. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Notably, a system without the auxiliary frequency features still yields satisfactory results in speech synthesis tasks. The open-source code of the proposed model is also made available online. Empirical studies suggest that modeling periodic signals as a given prior can significantly improve modeling performance and quality of generated samples, especially in speech synthesis tasks. The quantitative and qualitative evaluation results position QPNet among the top-performing models in the MUSAN speech synthesis benchmark. The model's ability to generate music from raw waveforms using auxiliary frequency features as a score also demonstrates its versatility. The execution efficiency of the proposed deep learning model is on par with other state-of-the-art architectures, making it suitable for numerous audio synthesis applications. The prototype of a synthesizer implemented with QPNet has been successfully integrated into a professional digital audio workstation software. The innovative architecture of the model may also be applied to the generative modeling of raw waveforms in other quasi-periodic signals. The relatively small number of parameters required by the model allows it to be deployed on mobile devices and cloud services. The execution speed and model flexibility make QPNet an ideal choice for numerous real-time and non-real-time audio synthesis use cases. The model's versatility in generating both musical and speech audio from raw waveforms further cements its position as the state-of-the-art WaveNet derivative. The relatively simple design and flexible auxiliary feature-based architecture of the model also provide opportunities for further exploration and innovation in the field of deep learning-based waveform generation. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Moreover, LGCN exhibits greater parameter efficiency and real-time inference capability, making it a more practical solution. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism proofs are provided for the occurrence of negative temperatures within closed systems, including proofs for the general case of quantum systems, based on the Boltzmann and microcanonic distributions. Additionally, specific examples of negative temperatures are presented, drawn from various fields, such as physics, biology, medicine, and astronomy, where they were previously misunderstood or mislabeled. Furthermore, discussions on the implementation and utilization of negative temperatures in research are also included. Finally, the rights and ethics surrounding the use of negative temperatures are addressed, as some individuals have been incorrectly attributing their own research on this topic. Additionally, the paper includes an open challenge for achieving negative brightness temperature in free-electron lasers. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In response, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. UniToPatho is unique in its comprehensive scope, covering a wide range of polyp types, sizes, and locations, along with varying levels of dysplasia, making it an invaluable asset for anyone seeking to advance the field through advanced computer-aided diagnosis techniques. Additionally, we've outlined initial results obtained using a deep learning model trained with this dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in both classification and grading tasks. UniToPatho and its associated protocols are now available for public access, enabling the continuous expansion of this valuable dataset through collaborations and data sharing. In line with these goals, we've established a dedicated webpage and are actively exploring ways to expand UniToPatho through partnerships and collaborations. We believe that open-access datasets like UniToPatho will contribute significantly to the advancement of computer-aided colorectal polyp detection, characterization, and diagnosis. To facilitate further research based on this dataset, we've set up a challenge focused on characterization and grading tasks; more details on this initiative can be found in the associated document. UniToPatho is an innovative initiative aimed at creating a comprehensive dataset that can propel the field of colorectal polyp characterization through advanced computer-aided diagnosis techniques. We're eager to collaborate with institutions, pathologists, and researchers to enhance this dataset, address the research questions outlined in the document, and explore new applications of deep learning models. If you're interested in contributing to UniToPatho or participating in related challenges, please don't hesitate to get in touch with us. We're open to incorporating whole-slide images and annotations from various sources, as well as exploring new annotation schemes and data sharing collaborations. UniToPatho has the potential to become a leading reference dataset for colorectal polyp characterization, and we invite everyone with a common goal to contribute

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. These advances, however, are not observed in high-data settings due to the dominance of audiologically biased speech recognition models. Our work paves the way for tackling speech-to-text challenges. Our code and models are available for public access. Despite advancements in machine learning, speech-to-text challenges persist, particularly in low-data settings and languages with limited transcription data availability. We explore zero-shot translation, leveraging linguistic similarities to facilitate the learning process. By extending this capability to speech, we enable the translation of spoken language across different tongues. While successful speech recognition relies on auditory features similar to those used in model training, our results show that zero-shot speech-to-text models perform subparly (up to -6.8 BLEU points) in comparison to similarly trained direct speech-to-text models. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. Our implementation shows that multipoles can offer a valuable alternative to traditional methods for computing optical forces. Due to their flexible nature, multipoles can easily be applied to examine the optical force exerted on particles with irregular shapes. Furthermore, we explore the civic of multipoles to describe the electromagnetic activity of particles versus their scattering behavior. Interestingly, we discover that there is no straightforward equivalence between scattering and electromagnetic multipoles. Consequently, merely measuring scattering patterns is insufficient to recover a particle's three-dimensional structure. This insight holds important implications for techniques that utilize multipoles to infer the morphology of scattered particles. Ultimately, our analysis highlights that the choice of multipoles affects predictions of optical force calculations. Given that the Mie theory is widely employed as a standard for describing the scattering and optical force calculations of spherical particles, we examine its behavior over a wide range of wavelength parameters. Our analysis covers up to 100 times the characteristic radius of the particle in question, which is relevant to applications involving sub-wavelength particles. Nonetheless, we discover that the Mie theory exhibits divergent behavior when calculating the quadrupolar contribution to scattering and optical force at wavelengths greater than 10 times the particle's radius. To address this issue, we develop a modified multipoles expansion scheme that allows the description of particle behavior within the Mie regime. Our proposed model involves introducing an additional term that accounts for the volume dipolar contribution, thereby circumventing the divergence problem. As a result, our modified multipoles expansion scheme can accurately describe the electromagnetic scattering behavior and optical force calculations within the Mie regime. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our approach and code are now publicly available for download. Moreover, several applications based on disease-aware image editing recently have been created. These models can be trained from scratch using our pre-trained models, which provide a starting point for further exploration in medical imaging enhancement. These models specifically focus on cardiac enlargement and can be adapted to other conditions such as pneumonia, cardiac enlargement, pleural effusion, and fractures by using the CheXpert dataset. Our research also has sparked significant interest in the medical imaging community. In response to the numerous inquiries and interest shown in our work, we have created several new training scenarios and models that solve several challenges in medical imaging enhancement. These solutions address key issues such as data privacy, limited available data for training models, and the complex nature of chest X-rays. These advancements have resulted in more realistic training scenarios, improved performance metrics, and enhanced user experience through our user-friendly interface.
